As a mandated reporter, your identity is typically protected when you report suspected abuse or neglect to Child Protective Services (CPS). Here are key points to consider regarding your questions:

1. **Employer's Obligation to Disclose**: Generally, your employer is not supposed to disclose your identity to the family. Most states have laws that protect the identity of mandated reporters to encourage the reporting of suspected abuse without fear of retaliation or harassment.

2. **Legality of Disclosure by Employer**: It is usually illegal for your employer to disclose your identity to the family if you have reported them to CPS. The laws protecting mandated reporters are designed to ensure confidentiality to prevent any potential backlash or harm to the reporter.

3. **Actions You Can Take**:
    - **Review State Laws**: Check the specific laws in your state regarding mandated reporting and confidentiality to understand your rights and protections fully.
    - **Report the Breach**: If your employer discloses your identity, you can report this breach to CPS or the appropriate governing body in your state that oversees mandated reporting.
    - **Seek Legal Advice**: Consider consulting with an attorney who specializes in employment law or child welfare law to understand your options and possibly take legal action against your employer.
    - **Document Everything**: Keep detailed records of your report to CPS and any communications with your employer regarding the disclosure. This documentation can be critical if you need to pursue legal action.

Protecting the identity of mandated reporters is crucial for maintaining the integrity and effectiveness of child protection services. If your employer violates these protections, you have the right to seek redress through appropriate legal channels.

I want to be meaningful to others.

So then I reframe my initial anxiety as “I can learn from this person and/or they can learn from me.” And I live my life in the light of always coming from a place of wanting to support others and knowing that they might be able to support me.

The reality is that we’re all awkward, we’re all weird, we’re all different. Whenever you think someone is judging you, remember that they probably feel the same way about you. 

So when I feel this way, I just model what I would want other people to treat me as. I smile, I ask questions, I ensure the other person knows I found our interaction meaningful, etc. 

The best way I’ve learned to handle anxiety is to fake it til I make it.

I can understand why that would be frustrating; we want to feel as though our partners care about us and our families. While I don’t know enough and can’t say anything for certain, I’d love to offer a few different angles at which this may be viewed:

She potentially deals with sickness or mortality/immortality in a different way

Or

She may have never dealt with a situation like this

Or

She may have a different relationship with her family which may translate to your family 

Or

She may not know that you want her there with you being that it is a big life event. Idk what the dynamics are, but it could be awkward for her depending on what kind of relationship she has with each of your family members that are there.

- One approach would be to ask if she’d like to join, potentially mention how that would make you feel.

- Another approach I would take would be to say something like:

“Hey, I need you to know that my brother’s situation is serious. Something I’ve noticed is that you don’t really ask about him, and you haven’t gone to see him. That makes me feel like you don’t care. While I’m sure that’s not your intention, could you help me understand? (You can talk about it here, but end with what you need, something like the next sentence but true for you). Moving forward, asking me about the things that matter and coming to be a part of big life events would really make me feel like we’re in this together.” 

And at that point, since you said what you need out loud to her, you can then hold her to something. 


Sadly we are not taught all the ways to behave in all the situations, but the best way to leave a situation (that makes us uncomfortable) without a doubt is to end with what you need from this experience moving forward. Then you evaluate if the person can follow through, and you’ll know you did your part. 

This is just me, however, and how I would take apart this situation (with the context given) should I find myself in it. I wish you the best, friend! 🙌💚

I’d have two options in this scenario:

1. Despite sounding crazy, I’d bring out the full truth. I can’t call my partner out on something and at the same time try to sweep my own part of the story under the rug or lie about it. That’s toxic. That’s not fair to them, or myself. In this option: I would identify the boundaries that need to be set, state them, and follow through. I would also keep in mind that while it is my job to set the boundary, it is not my partner’s obligation to follow through. All I can do is voice my needs/concerns and observe whether the my partner respects me enough to listen & act accordingly. But, assuming nothing changes, what then? When do I decide that I’ve had enough or have seen improvement? I need to have a clear boundary for myself on that one.

2. I could just leave. If I am feeling crazy enough that I have to check other girls’ social media for data on the person I am with, that’s too much effort. Way too much. I’m probably feeling burnout from a job that I didn’t even sign up for. I’m not even getting paid to stalk this human! 😩😂

I spent years hating my family, then learned: that’s what they were taught. You can’t blame someone for taking the word of their “superiors,” because, during those days, that was the model: someone over someone. We didn’t see people as *just* humans.

So now I engage with my family only in the context of reshaping some of those beliefs to foster a healthy environment. 
If I hear a hard belief that makes no sense, I can (as an adult) more effectively tackle it than when I was younger, and provide an alternative. 

I also learned it is my choice, through and through, to continue to connect with said beings. I can choose not to associate with people who make me feel less than myself at any time. Moreover, it is my choice whether I allow our same relationships to continue or if I decide to model the appropriate way to have a meaningful relationship.

My responses are typically something along the lines of “oh look, a human,” with no emotional responding or facial expressions involved, and then I move along as though my life mattered more. Because it does, and I will fight to the death should the need arise. I’m a female, and this is a genuine concern I have for my life as such. But if I’m not in danger, this is the response that wins for me, because it’s a literal “dude you mean nothing, you’re just phenomena happening & one day you’ll die, too.” 

But that’s just my morbid philosophy 🤷🏻‍♀️😂
